I’ve been feeling really off for about a year now. Most days I’m just…low. It’s like everything’s gone flat. Things I used to enjoy—hunting trips, watching games with my buddies, even messing around with my kids—don’t really do anything for me anymore. I drag myself to the yard, and by mid‑shift I’m wiped out, even if I slept a full night. My wife says I just sit there staring at the TV, not really in it. I catch myself thinking it’d be easier if I just didn’t wake up, or that everyone would be better off without me, though I haven’t planned anything.

But then there’ll be these stretches, like this past month, where I flip the other way. I’ll be buzzing, talking a mile a minute, jumping from one idea to the next. I start extra shifts, projects around the house, all at once. I barely sleep a couple hours and feel like I don’t need it. My mood swings fast—one minute I’m joking around, the next I’m snapping at my wife over nothing. My sex drive goes way up during those times too, like I’m constantly keyed up. It hasn’t wrecked my job, but it’s definitely made things tense at home.
D009-D003_h004.question_a:
It’s kind of like I’ve been living in two different gears.

Most of this past year I’ve been stuck in the low one. I wake up feeling heavy and low, even when I’ve slept all night. I don’t really enjoy anything anymore—not work, not fishing with my buddies, not even hanging out with my kids. It’s like the good feeling part of my brain is shut off. I’m dragging all the time, almost like I’ve got the flu that never ends. I still go to the yard because I have to, but I’ve called out more, missed overtime, and my foreman’s noticed I’m slower and zoning out. I get these thoughts like, “What’s the point? Maybe everybody’s better off without me,” but I haven’t made any plans.

Then about a month ago, I flipped into the opposite. I hardly sleep—maybe three hours—and I don’t even feel tired. I talk so fast my wife tells me to slow down because she can’t keep up. My mind jumps around, I start a dozen projects at home and at work, and I feel wired and on edge—super upbeat one minute, snapping at people the next. My sex drive shoots way up; I’m all over my wife, way more than usual. But this only started in the last few years, not when I was a kid.

Lately it’s just been more intense, with me feeling revved up, snappy, and more pushy about sex with my wife, but that “on” feeling has basically been there my whole life.

I guess the main thing is my mood and energy are all over the place. For about a year now I’ve felt mostly…flat and heavy. I go to my interpreting jobs and I can do them, but everything feels like I’m moving through mud. I used to love the work and chatting with my Deaf clients, but now even when something should be funny or sweet, I just feel nothing. At home my husband says I seem “checked out.” I’m exhausted all the time; dishes pile up, laundry sits, I cancel plans a lot.

At my lowest, I’ve thought very concretely about ending things. I’ve picked out a place near the river and imagined the time of day, even how I’d make it look like an accident. Those thoughts scare me, but they also feel weirdly calm.

Then there was this stretch about a month long where I was the opposite. I was snapping at everyone over tiny things, pacing around the house, starting extra projects at work—volunteering for extra interpreting shifts, planning new workshops—like I couldn’t sit still. I barely slept for several nights in a row and it didn’t bother me; I just kept going. My husband said I was talking nonstop, jumping from topic to topic, and he couldn’t get a word in. I didn’t feel “bad” then, just wired and on edge.
D009-D003_h005.question_a:
It’s like I have two very different gears.

About a year ago I slipped into this low gear and just never really came out of it. I wake up feeling heavy and sad every day, like there’s a gray film over everything. Things I used to enjoy—interpreting at the college, hanging out with my Deaf friends, even being with my husband—just feel flat. I go through the motions, but there’s no spark. I’m exhausted all the time; even taking a shower or prepping for class feels like climbing a hill. I’ve fallen behind on emails and lesson prep, and I’ve had to cut my hours because I just can’t keep up. I’ve also spent a lot of time thinking about ending my life—where I’d do it, how to make sure my husband wouldn’t be the one to find me.

But about a month this past spring I flipped into the opposite state. I was on edge and snappy over nothing, pacing around the apartment, unable to sit still. I slept maybe three hours a night and didn’t feel tired at all. My mind was racing with ideas for new interpreting workshops, online classes, side projects—I actually started several at once. At work I couldn’t stop talking, voice and sign both, filling every silence; meetings turned into me running the show. That kind of revved-up feeling only happens in those “up” stretches—when I’m not in one of those phases, I’m not like that, and I definitely wasn’t like that as a kid.
D009-D003_h005.question_b:
If I look back, I’ve always been this way. My mom says even in elementary school I “never had an off switch” — talking nonstop, fidgeting, staying up late reading with a flashlight and still bouncing off the walls the next day. I remember lying in bed at 10 or 11 years old, mind racing so fast I just couldn’t shut it off, but I’d still get up and go, like sleep was optional.

As an adult, it’s the same, just more obvious at work. Interpreting should be about pacing with the speaker, but I tend to sign too fast, jump in early, and I get this almost physical discomfort if there’s a pause. I fill silence with talking, with my hands or my mouth. I constantly start extra projects, volunteer for extra assignments, and I can’t seem to sit still in staff meetings. My thoughts skip around; I’m easily distracted and always half‑doing three things at once.

About a year ago, though, I hit this long slump — feeling low pretty much every day, not enjoying time with my husband or even signing, which I usually love. I feel drained just getting out of bed. I’ve had moments where I’ve thought through, in detail, how I might end things — when, where, and how — even though I haven’t acted on it.

About a year ago I had this stretch, maybe three weeks, where I felt incredible. I’d wake up after three, four hours of sleep and feel totally refreshed, buzzing. My mind was going a mile a minute, ideas on how to “fix” the whole agency, launch new community programs, write a book about grief. I honestly felt like I’d been chosen for something big, like I had this special gift for changing people’s lives. I talked nonstop in meetings, pacing around the room, wringing my hands, unable to sit through home visits. I’d start five projects at once, flit between them, get distracted mid-sentence. That kind of hyper, talky, wired version of me only shows up in these “up” spells; as a kid I was quiet, if anything.

Most of this past year, though, I’ve been the opposite. Numb. It’s like someone turned the volume down on all my feelings. I drag myself through my caseload, exhausted no matter how much I sleep. I’ve been calling in sick because just getting dressed feels like climbing a mountain. When I do sleep, I wake up from horrible, vivid nightmares about my husband’s death, heart racing, and then I’m even more drained the next day.

Stuff I used to love, like trail running with my dog or even playing with the kittens at the clinic, just feels flat. I move like I’m underwater—coworkers joke I’m “slow motion” when I’m walking down the hall or reaching for meds. I’m exhausted all the time, even if I sleep 9–10 hours. On my days off I barely get off the couch, and I cry over nothing—commercials, a client’s dog getting better, anything. It’s made it hard to keep up at work and with basic chores.

Then, about three months ago, I flipped into this other state for a while. I barely slept—maybe three hours a night—and didn’t feel tired. My mind was going a mile a minute, jumping from reorganizing the med room to planning a side business to texting people non‑stop. I was talking so fast my coworkers had to tell me to slow down. I couldn’t sit still, always pacing or cleaning something. I’d get super upbeat and then randomly snap and get really irritable. Outside of those “up” times, I don’t have that racing mind, rapid talking, or the no‑sleep thing—those only show up in those high spells.
D009-D003_h025.question_b:
I’ve always been “go go go” since I was a kid. My mom used to say I was like a wind‑up toy that never ran down. Even back in elementary school I talked fast, jumped from one thing to another, and could stay up half the night reading or drawing and still be buzzing the next day. That’s kind of just…stayed the same into adulthood. I’m constantly fidgeting at the clinic, pacing between rooms, starting one task and then another before I finish the first. My brain feels like it’s got ten radio stations on at once—racing thoughts, jumping topics, and I talk so quickly my coworkers ask me to slow down. I honestly don’t feel like I ever really need much sleep; I fight going to bed and then wake up wired.

Over the last year or so, though, it’s like I hit a wall. I stopped caring about the stuff I used to love—trail running, baking, even playing with my dog. I move slower, even just walking down the hall, and simple things feel like wading through mud. I’m exhausted all the time even when I sleep enough, and I’ve had days where I just start crying at work for no obvious reason. That’s been messing with my job and my social life a lot.
